records.our_prose: Eggplant grows for a long time and likes steady feeding, but the timing matters. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the soil before you plant. Then wait: once the first little eggplants have set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer, and again a few weeks later. Going heavy on fertilizer too early gives you a big leafy plant with few flowers, so save the feeding for after the fruit starts forming.

records.our_prose: Eggplant is a moderately heavy feeder over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen once the first fruits have set and again three to four weeks later through the harvest. Hold the nitrogen back before fruit set, since too much early on drives leafy growth and few flowers; the time to push it is after the plant starts carrying fruit. Pair feeding with steady moisture, because fertilizer only helps a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

records.our_prose: Start eggplant seeds indoors about 8 weeks before transplanting (UMD uses 8 to 10 week old transplants), with bottom heat of 75 to 85°F for fast, even germination. Eggplant needs a longer, warmer start than tomato and is set out later, once nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Choose sturdy transplants up to a foot tall with stems about pencil thick, and set plant supports at planting. Direct sowing is practical only in the longest, warmest regions; everywhere else this is a transplant crop.
